Introduction

So, after a debugging session the other day, I was having some shower thoughts regarding early userspace and initrd.

Linux initramfs supports unpacking CPIO, a stupid, simple, standardized format. In the discussion on whether to support TAR instead, much emphasize has been put on the fact that CPIO is standardized and less fragmented.

Luckily, Linux (the kernel) includes its own tool to produce the specific variant of the standard that it happens to implement. The standard CPIO tool is possibly the most cursed archiver under the SUN.

In the old DOS/WinDOS world, ZIP was probably the most wide spread and well known archive format, being displaced to some extend by the rise of RAR during the 2000s.

Because of the design of the format, ZIP lends itself to all kinds of polyglot trickery. Way back when, self extracting ZIP archives where a thing, EXE/ZIP polyglots that can be run and unpack themselves, which is useful if you don't have an archiver installed.

I don't think I need to explain where I am going with this, here is the resulting ZIP archive I built:

Download boot.zip

It is a completely normal ZIP archive, containing its own source code needed to build itself from scratch: 

$ unzip -t boot.zip
Archive:  boot.zip
    testing: boot/ZIPHEAD.COM         OK
    testing: boot/MESSAGE.TXT         OK
    testing: common/asm.h             OK
    testing: common/multiboot.h       OK
    testing: common/zip.h             OK
    testing: multiboot/console.c      OK
    testing: multiboot/console.h      OK
    testing: multiboot/multiboot.c    OK
    testing: multiboot/string.S       OK
    testing: setup/a20.S              OK
    testing: setup/disk.S             OK
    testing: setup/entry16.S          OK
    testing: setup/entry32.S          OK
    testing: setup/mbload.S           OK
    testing: setup/mem.S              OK
    testing: setup/setup.ld           OK
    testing: util/fixhdr.c            OK
    testing: util/zipglue.c           OK
    testing: util/zippack.c           OK
    testing: mk.sh                    OK
    testing: README.txt               OK
    testing: MESSAGE.txt              OK
    testing: LICENSE.txt              OK
No errors detected in compressed data of boot.zip.

A particularly interesting file here is boot/ZIPHEAD.COM, that contains executable code that is run when booting the archive.

You need to fix the execute permissions of mk.sh after unpacking, and you will need a copy of Zlib installed for the tools. Running mk.sh from it's directory should leave you with a fresh copy of the bootable ZIP archive.

The simplest way to run it, is to just pass it to Qemu direct kernel boot: 

$ qemu-system-i386 -kernel boot.zip

"That's easy" you might say, "Qemu supports Multiboot, that ZIPHEAD.COM is uncompressed, at the beginning of the archive and has a Multiboot header in it!"

Yes, that's all true! But this ZIP archive also brings it's own boot loader along. You can try putting it on a floppy and throw that in front of Qemu: 

$ dd if=/dev/zero of=floppy.img count=2880
$ dd if=boot.zip of=floppy.img conv=notrunc
$ qemu-system-i386 -fda floppy.img

The first 512 bytes of the archive contain a valid boot sector that loads some more code from the second sector and then bootstraps itself into highmem with the A20 enabled and 32 bit protected mode set up.

You can also put it on a hard drive too, it detects what INT 13h drive it's been loaded from and dutifully queries the disk geometry.

If you care to try, you can also dump it on a real floppy and stuff it into a PC:

That's a Pentium MMX by the way, but I also tried an i486 DX2 and an Am386DX-40, just to be sure. My 486 had me hold my breath for a moment, it has a spectacularly slow floppy drive. The text on screen is from the file boot/MESSAGE.TXT

"But that's not special either" you might respond, "ZIPs are read from the back, you can just put anything you want in front, so you put a boot sector there!"

That is sadly not quite true anymore, I'll get to that. But for now, lets take a look at the first couple bytes of that archive together and we'll see the real party trick: 

$ xxd -g 1 -l 128 boot.zip
00000000: 50 4b 03 04 0a 00 02 80 00 00 eb 44 e4 2e 41 0f  PK.........D..A.
00000010: 01 8f 0a 09 00 00 0a 09 00 00 10 00 00 00 62 6f  ..............bo
00000020: 6f 74 2f 5a 49 50 48 45 41 44 2e 43 4f 4d 00 90  ot/ZIPHEAD.COM..
00000030: 02 b0 ad 1b 03 00 01 00 fb 4f 51 e4 30 00 10 00  .........OQ.0...
00000040: 00 00 10 00 bd 72 10 00 bd 72 10 00 31 03 10 00  .....r...r..1...
00000050: fa fc 31 c0 89 c4 8e d8 8e c0 8e d0 ea 61 7c 00  ..1..........a|.
00000060: 00 bf 00 06 b9 00 02 f3 aa 88 16 98 06 be 0f 7d  ...............}
00000070: e8 8c 00 b8 00 f0 89 c1 50 9d 9c 58 a8 02 74 4a  ........P..X..tJ

The ASCII P stands for Phil ( not Picard ), as in Phil Katz, followed by 03h and 04h. What you are looking at, is a completely valid ZIP local file header for boot/ZIPHEAD.COM

Oh, and those other bytes there after the ZIP header: 02 b0 ad 1b, if you flip them around to human endian, it reads 1BADB002. That's the Multiboot magic :-)

The 16 bit real mode code starts right after the Multiboot header, at offset 00000050. If you are feeling a little confused, so is the file utility: 

$ file boot.zip
boot.zip: DOS/MBR boot sector; partition 1 : ID=0xd, active 0xcd, start-CHS (0x7
2,19,7), end-CHS (0x388,254,6), startsector 2147916342, 243810273 sectors; parti
tion 2 : ID=0x60, active 0x9c, start-CHS (0x366,6,3), end-CHS (0x3f7,49,18), sta
rtsector 2298911798, 4154016209 sectors; partition 4 : ID=0xf8, active 0xe1, sta
rt-CHS (0x2,184,1), end-CHS (0x313,6,13), startsector 3277940231, 0 sectors

If you take a closer look at the first line of the hex dump, you might be able to spot the jump instruction that makes this little magic trick possible. Luckily, Phil Katz' initials are valid opcodes. The Multiboot entry point is much further into the file at offset 00000331.

ZIP Archives Revisited

Here's a picture you probably recognize from the Wikipedia article about the ZIP format . This here is a local copy, Wikimedia Commons hosts the original with attribution and licensing information .

Much like a TAR or CPIO archive, a ZIP file is an amalgamation of tightly packed files with a short header in front, specifying the full file path and other meta data: 

typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t version;
	uint16_t flags;
	uint16_t method;
	uint16_t modtime;
	uint16_t moddate;
	uint32_t checksum;
	uint32_t compsize;
	uint32_t origsize;
	uint16_t namelength;
	uint16_t extralength;
	char name[namelength];
	uint8_t extra[extralength];
} __attribute__((packed)) zip_entry_t;

The timestamps are DOS datetime, the checksum is a CRC-32, there are no attributes or permission bits, we are thoroughly in DOS land. Directories are implied by the file paths.

Nit pick Yes, I know, the central directory has a field where "internal" and "external" attributes can be stored, whose meaning depends on the OS ID byte in the version field. Later versions of the format added an extension to support directories. Good luck making use of that in a portable way that can be understood by different archivers across different WinDOS versions and Unix clones.

Unlike TAR or CPIO, there is a central directory in the end, with a listing of all of the file headers and back references to the file in the archive. Unlike traditional file formats that have are started by a header, ZIP is terminated by a footer.

The reason for this is twofold:

  • the archive can be generated in a single, forward pass (collecting the directory in memory).
  • Accessing a single file in the archive can be done quickly, by looking through the directory and going directly to the file.

That last part was especially important in the days when ZIP archives would be split over several floppies. To access a file, just scan the directory on the last floppy, then tell the user what floppy to insert to get the file.

By comparison, accessing a file in a tarball requires linearly scanning over the whole thing (which, on the other hand, is preferable for tape drives , where TAR originates).

Polyglot Trickery

ZIP archives are meant to be read from the back, the footer points to the central directory, the directory points to the files. In theory, the archiver shouldn't care if there happens to be a gap between two files, containing something else or if there is something else in the front of the archive, like a file header for a different file format.

The local file headers also supports up to 64k of "extra" stuff between the header and the file data, the footer has "comment" at the end, also up to 64k.

If you look at the footer for a second, you might spot an interesting design flaw: 

typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t disknum;
	uint16_t diskstart;
	uint16_t num_dir_entries;
	uint16_t total_dir_entries;
	uint32_t dir_size;
	uint32_t dir_start;
	uint16_t comment_length;
	uint8_t comment[comment_length];
} __attribute__((packed)) zip_end_t;

it is variable size, an archiver needs to find it looking from the back, but the magic and the size are both stored before the variable sized comment field. Ask yourself this for a moment: how would you implement this in an archiver? Demanding that there is no comment? Reading the last 64k plus some change and scanning it? From which direction? What if there is another valid footer inside the comment field of the footer? Depending on how an implementation deals with this, a specifically crafted archive can appear to contain different files when viewed with different archivers.

Trying to make the format extensible ended up building a whole lot of foot guns in there. And we are not even talking about the plethora of extensions that have been tacked on to the official specification over the years.

Many modern implementations decided to save themselves a lot of headaches and just treat ZIP archives the same way as tarballs, linearly scanning them from the front instead. They expect the archive to start with a local header, skipping by the size MUST lead to the next entry or finally, the central directory. They reject any archives where this is not possible. This effectively prevents a lot of polyglot trick fuckery, but at the cost of rendering possibly valid archives unreadable.

For the self booting ZIP archive, the challenge thus becomes: the archive MUST start with a local file header, there cannot be any gaps, everything must be properly contained inside files.

The easy part: Multiboot

Anybody who has ever looked at a DIY toy OS tutorial has probably stumbled across The Multiboot Specification , the possibly easiest and most beginner friendly way to get a program running on bare metal x86.

The multiboot spec originates in the GNU/FSF ecosystem and is implemented by boot loaders like GRUB or Qemu direct kernel boot. SYSLINUX supports it via a plugin. There is a draft for an over engineered 2nd version, that also supports MIPS, but this is of no concert to us here.

A Multiboot 1 compliant kernel simply contains the magic value 0x1BADB002 somewhere in the first in the first 8k. This is followed by flags and a checksum (all 3 must add up to zero). Depending on the flags, additional fields may follow.

The kernel itself can be an ELF file from which the loader extracts load address and entry point. The kernel is run in 32 bit protected mode with flat segments (base=0, limit=4G) and the A20 gate enabled.

Nit pick The specification actually doesn't mandate ELF, but rather "an ordinary 32-bit executable file in whatever file format the operating system normally uses.", it then goes on to specify optional fields in the info struct for either ELF or a.out. In theory, it should also be possible for a boot loader to only support PE and not be in violation of the spec.

Alternatively to a plain old ELF file, the kernel can also specify the memory layout manually (indicated via a flag), allowing flat binaries or other file formats to be loaded. The extended header looks like this: 

typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint32_t flags;
	uint32_t checksum;
	uint32_t hdr_addr;
	uint32_t load_addr;
	uint32_t load_end_addr;
	uint32_t bss_end_addr;
	uint32_t entry_point;
} mb_header_t;

The hdr_addr specifies the in-memory address of the header after loading the file, using this and the file offset where the header was found, the other addresses can be converted back to file offsets by the loader.

This way, the load_addr and load_end_addr are used to figure out what parts of the file to load where into memory. If the bss_end_addr is past that, the loader zero-fills it, before finally jumping to entry_point to run the kernel.

The Multiboot compliant loader also sets up a structure with system information (e.g. memory map, APM tables), kernel command line, etc… and passes the pointer to the kernel (via register EBX, magic value 0x2BADB002 in EAX).

Making a Multiboot bootable ZIP archive is trivial. Simply pack a flat binary with a Multiboot header as uncompressed file binary, make sure it is at the beginning and the addresses line up. An external tool can then fix up the headers, so that the whole archive is loaded.

For any practical applications, it would make sense to stop right here, but we're not here for "practical" or "sane".

Making it BIOS bootable

On an IBM compatible machine, the BIOS iterates over the installed drives, loads the first sector from each (to location 0x7c00), until it finds one where the first sector ends with 0xaa55. It then jumps to the first byte.

Disks that are formatted with a filesystem, typically have a header in the beginning that starts with a jump instruction across the header into the bootstrap code that follows. The DOS MBR format opts to instead store the partition table at the end of the first sector and all the code in the front.

If we stuff a BIOS boot signature into the ZIP archive, at least parts of the ZIP local file header will be executed, the first few bytes are a mandated magic value and we cannot just put a jump instruction there.

The puzzle exercise now becomes, filling the header fields with values that make sense but also happen to be valid 8086 opcodes. At least, until we hit something that can be abused as a free-form field that we can stuff a jump into.

Let's take a look at that hex dump again: 

00000000: 50 4b 03 04 0a 00 02 80 00 00 eb 44 e4 2e 41 0f  PK.........D..A.
00000010: 01 8f 0a 09 00 00 0a 09 00 00 10 00 00 00 62 6f  ..............bo
00000020: 6f 74 2f 5a 49 50 48 45 41 44 2e 43 4f 4d 00 90  ot/ZIPHEAD.COM..

I've tried to highlight the relevant header up to the jump instruction: 0xeb is a relative jump with a single byte immediate argument.

If we take a look again at the header structure, we can make out what fields those bytes correspond to: 

typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t version;
	uint16_t flags;
	uint16_t method;
	uint16_t modtime;
	………

The timestamp is the first best place where we can put a jump instruction. The 0xeb relative jump works out to 8:30-ish in the morning, give or take the jump distance.

The two bytes in front of the modtime are compression method. We really, really want to have 0x0000 here, i.e. uncompressed, so that an archiver doesn't choke on the file data.

The first four bytes are the magic value of the format, we don't have any choice what to put here either, it has to be "PK\03\04". The version and flags fields are the only places where we have some creative freedom.

If we run the file through a dissassembler and take a look at the first few bytes, we'll end up with this: 

$ objdump -D -m i8086 -b binary ./boot.zip

./boot.zip:     file format binary


Disassembly of section .data:

00000000 <.data>:
       0:       50                      push   %ax
       1:       4b                      dec    %bx
       2:       03 04                   add    (%si),%ax
       4:       0a 00                   or     (%bx,%si),%al
       6:       02 80 00 00             add    0x0(%bx,%si),%al
       a:       eb 44                   jmp    0x50

This is AT&T syntax, source operands are left, destination on the right. We use GNU tools in this household, deal with it.

Anything that just fiddles around with a register doesn't really hurt us. Same goes for memory reads. We don't have memory protection, no matter what we access, there won't be any faults, the only memory mapped hardware around should be the frame buffer.

Memory writes are another story. Worst case, we could shoot up the interrupt vectors, the BIOS RAM areas (BDA, EBDA), or shadowed option ROMs.

The P for Phil also happens to also decode to push %ax. If the BIOS leaves us with a somewhat sane stack pointer, the push instruction should hopefully not mess anything up. It is part of the ZIP magic and thus unavoidable.

The version field is itself actually structured, containing a decimal encoded version number, followed by an OS ID byte. If we set it to 0x000a (stored as little endian), this decodes to version 1.0 on MS DOS.

0x0a is an orb, version 1.1 would be double byte sized, version 0.8 and 0.9 would be register direct and not touch the memory. An address of BX + SI is the result of a mod-reg-r/m field with all zeros.

We could try to code golf our way into consuming at least part of the flags as well, but low-valued, "harmless" opcodes that result in sane versions are sparse. Also, some version numbers change the meaning how an archiver is supposed to interpret the file. Also also, mod-reg-r/m combinations in the OS code field quickly end up as an undefined OS ID. Also also also, we have the method as well, that has to be 0x0000, which would result in a memory write if executed. We have to consume that somehow, rather than running it.

So for the flags, I came up with 0x8002 (stored as little endian). The lowest, set bit has a compression method dependent meaning, currently only defined for LZMA (14), deflate (8) and implode (6). For uncompressed (method 0) there is no defined meaning (the specification just ignores that part, it doesn't use nasty words like undefined). For deflate it would mean that maximum compression was used.

The MSB is specified as "reserved for use by PKWARE", whatever they chose to put there, if they ever chose anything at all. Most imporanly, the opcode 0x02 decodes to a single byte, indirect add, and in the mod-reg-r/m, the MSB tells the CPU to consume another 2 bytes of immediate DISPlacement. This is how we can get rid of the compression method.

At this point, we've made it! We reached the modtime field that we can just stuff a jump into.

Drawing the rest of the owl: Multiboot on foot

Once we've made it past the header, we are in 16 bit real mode. We just need to go through all of the neccessary steps to set up the environment that the Multiboot code expects:

  • Initialization (setup segments, clear scratch memory)
  • Figure out what kind of CPU we are running on
    • We need at least an i386, so we can actually run 32 bit code
    • The CPUID instruction was added to the Pentium and later 486, so we can't use that
    • We need to tickle undefined bits in the FLAGS register and watch what happens
  • Query disk parameters, load additional boot code past the first sector
    • We need the C/H/S geometry to sanely read past the first track
    • For simplicity, work with LBA and convert to C/H/S bit confetti for INT 13h as needed
  • Detect available memory
    • Memory below 1M via INT 12h
    • If supported, high memory via INT 15h, AX=E801h to query memory before and after the (possible) ISA memory hole at 15M
    • If that fails, fallback to INT 15h, AH=88h to get a lump sum of available high memory
    • If supported, get a detailed memory map via INT 15h, AX=E820h. This already uses the format specified by the Multiboot spec, just slap an extra size value in front of every entry.
  • Turn on the A20 gate
    • Check if memory location 0000:0600 (=0x0600) and ffff:0610 (=0x100600) overlap or not
    • Try BIOS INT 15h, AX=2401h
    • If that fails, try talking to the keyboard controller directly
    • If that fails, try SYSCTL A register
  • Load a GDT and set up 16 bit unreal mode
    • To actually access high memory, we need to get rid of the 64k segment limits
    • We need to stay in real-ish mode, so we can keep using INT 13h
  • Load the rest of the archive into high memory
  • Jump to the Multiboot entry point
    • Re-enter protected mode, 32 bit code segment
    • Cobble the rest of the Multiboot info struct together
    • Leap-of-faith into highmem

This might sound like a lot, but in the current version, the actual code boils down to 817 bytes. That includes all the headers (ZIP, multiboot), the rather bulky GDT. But it is still quite a lot and outside the scope of this post anyway, I might pick some interesting parts out of it for some follow-up posts (watch this space?).

Through the Looking Glass

The Multiboot entry code re-loads the GDT, but this time using the highmem location, and sets up a stack after the archive. The size is extracted from the Multiboot header. Knowing the start address, the C code can then iterate over itself to locate and access files in the archive.

Some linker script trickery is used to tie it all into one blob, but with the GDT and Multiboot header visible from both lomem and highmem code at different locations.

At this point, you might be inclined to actually read the source code in the ZIP archive. There are lots of comments trying to explain what is going on.

There's a README that points out the structure of the code with suggestions where to start reading. I decided to keep it readable rather than stuff it all into a single sector. Self-modifying trickery is kept to a minimum (to safe some space, the function to enter unreal mode modifies itself, the code is run twice, courtesy of a misdirected ret, entering protected mode the first time round, leaving it again and restoring the segment registers on the second run, before returning for real).

Code in the archive and this blog posts have been written with assistance from:

  • Tegernseer Hell
  • Gouryella et al

If you poke around in the code and have any suggestions for improvements, or otherwise do anything interesting with it, please let me know.

Have fun!

Unlike traditional file formats that have are started by a header, ZIP is terminated by a footer. The reason for this is twofold: the archive can be generated in a single, forward pass (collecting the directory in memory). Accessing a single file in the archive can be done quickly, by looking through the directory and going directly to the file. That last part was especially important in the days when ZIP archives would be split over several floppies. To access a file, just scan the directory on the last floppy, then tell the user what floppy to insert to get the file. By comparison, accessing a file in a tarball requires linearly scanning over the whole thing (which, on the other hand, is preferable for tape drives , where TAR originates). Polyglot Trickery ZIP archives are meant to be read from the back, the footer points to the central directory, the directory points to the files. In theory, the archiver shouldn't care if there happens to be a gap between two files, containing something else or if there is something else in the front of the archive, like a file header for a different file format. The local file headers also supports up to 64k of "extra" stuff between the header and the file data, the footer has "comment" at the end, also up to 64k. If you look at the footer for a second, you might spot an interesting design flaw: typedef struct { uint32_t magic; uint16_t disknum; uint16_t diskstart; uint16_t num_dir_entries; uint16_t total_dir_entries; uint32_t dir_size; uint32_t dir_start; uint16_t comment_length; uint8_t comment[comment_length]; } __attribute__((packed)) zip_end_t; it is variable size, an archiver needs to find it looking from the back, but the magic and the size are both stored before the variable sized comment field. Ask yourself this for a moment: how would you implement this in an archiver? Demanding that there is no comment? Reading the last 64k plus some change and scanning it? From which direction? What if there is another valid footer inside the comment field of the footer? Depending on how an implementation deals with this, a specifically crafted archive can appear to contain different files when viewed with different archivers. Trying to make the format extensible ended up building a whole lot of foot guns in there. And we are not even talking about the plethora of extensions that have been tacked on to the official specification over the years. Many modern implementations decided to save themselves a lot of headaches and just treat ZIP archives the same way as tarballs, linearly scanning them from the front instead. They expect the archive to start with a local header, skipping by the size MUST lead to the next entry or finally, the central directory. They reject any archives where this is not possible. This effectively prevents a lot of polyglot trick fuckery, but at the cost of rendering possibly valid archives unreadable. For the self booting ZIP archive, the challenge thus becomes: the archive MUST start with a local file header, there cannot be any gaps, everything must be properly contained inside files. The easy part: Multiboot Anybody who has ever looked at a DIY toy OS tutorial has probably stumbled across The Multiboot Specification , the possibly easiest and most beginner friendly way to get a program running on bare metal x86. The multiboot spec originates in the GNU/FSF ecosystem and is implemented by boot loaders like GRUB or Qemu direct kernel boot. SYSLINUX supports it via a plugin. There is a draft for an over engineered 2nd version, that also supports MIPS, but this is of no concert to us here. A Multiboot 1 compliant kernel simply contains the magic value 0x1BADB002 somewhere in the first in the first 8k. This is followed by flags and a checksum (all 3 must add up to zero). Depending on the flags, additional fields may follow. The kernel itself can be an ELF file from which the loader extracts load address and entry point. The kernel is run in 32 bit protected mode with flat segments (base=0, limit=4G) and the A20 gate enabled. Nit pick The specification actually doesn't mandate ELF, but rather "an ordinary 32-bit executable file in whatever file format the operating system normally uses.", it then goes on to specify optional fields in the info struct for either ELF or a.out. In theory, it should also be possible for a boot loader to only support PE and not be in violation of the spec. Alternatively to a plain old ELF file, the kernel can also specify the memory layout manually (indicated via a flag), allowing flat binaries or other file formats to be loaded. The extended header looks like this: typedef struct { uint32_t magic; uint32_t flags; uint32_t checksum; uint32_t hdr_addr; uint32_t load_addr; uint32_t load_end_addr; uint32_t bss_end_addr; uint32_t entry_point; } mb_header_t; The hdr_addr specifies the in-memory address of the header after loading the file, using this and the file offset where the header was found, the other addresses can be converted back to file offsets by the loader. This way, the load_addr and load_end_addr are used to figure out what parts of the file to load where into memory. If the bss_end_addr is past that, the loader zero-fills it, before finally jumping to entry_point to run the kernel. The Multiboot compliant loader also sets up a structure with system information (e.g. memory map, APM tables), kernel command line, etc… and passes the pointer to the kernel (via register EBX, magic value 0x2BADB002 in EAX). Making a Multiboot bootable ZIP archive is trivial. Simply pack a flat binary with a Multiboot header as uncompressed file binary, make sure it is at the beginning and the addresses line up. An external tool can then fix up the headers, so that the whole archive is loaded. For any practical applications, it would make sense to stop right here, but we're not here for "practical" or "sane". Making it BIOS bootable On an IBM compatible machine, the BIOS iterates over the installed drives, loads the first sector from each (to location 0x7c00), until it finds one where the first sector ends with 0xaa55. It then jumps to the first byte. Disks that are formatted with a filesystem, typically have a header in the beginning that starts with a jump instruction across the header into the bootstrap code that follows. The DOS MBR format opts to instead store the partition table at the end of the first sector and all the code in the front. If we stuff a BIOS boot signature into the ZIP archive, at least parts of the ZIP local file header will be executed, the first few bytes are a mandated magic value and we cannot just put a jump instruction there. The puzzle exercise now becomes, filling the header fields with values that make sense but also happen to be valid 8086 opcodes. At least, until we hit something that can be abused as a free-form field that we can stuff a jump into. Let's take a look at that hex dump again: 00000000: 50 4b 03 04 0a 00 02 80 00 00 eb 44 e4 2e 41 0f PK.........D..A. 00000010: 01 8f 0a 09 00 00 0a 09 00 00 10 00 00 00 62 6f ..............bo 00000020: 6f 74 2f 5a 49 50 48 45 41 44 2e 43 4f 4d 00 90 ot/ZIPHEAD.COM.. I've tried to highlight the relevant header up to the jump instruction: 0xeb is a relative jump with a single byte immediate argument. If we take a look again at the header structure, we can make out what fields those bytes correspond to: typedef struct { uint32_t magic; uint16_t version; uint16_t flags; uint16_t method; uint16_t modtime; ……… The timestamp is the first best place where we can put a jump instruction. The 0xeb relative jump works out to 8:30-ish in the morning, give or take the jump distance. The two bytes in front of the modtime are compression method. We really, really want to have 0x0000 here, i.e. uncompressed, so that an archiver doesn't choke on the file data. The first four bytes are the magic value of the format, we don't have any choice what to put here either, it has to be "PK\03\04". The version and flags fields are the only places where we have some creative freedom. If we run the file through a dissassembler and take a look at the first few bytes, we'll end up with this: $ objdump -D -m i8086 -b binary ./boot.zip ./boot.zip: file format binary Disassembly of section .data: 00000000 <.data>: 0: 50 push %ax 1: 4b dec %bx 2: 03 04 add (%si),%ax 4: 0a 00 or (%bx,%si),%al 6: 02 80 00 00 add 0x0(%bx,%si),%al a: eb 44 jmp 0x50 This is AT&T syntax, source operands are left, destination on the right. We use GNU tools in this household, deal with it. Anything that just fiddles around with a register doesn't really hurt us. Same goes for memory reads. We don't have memory protection, no matter what we access, there won't be any faults, the only memory mapped hardware around should be the frame buffer. Memory writes are another story. Worst case, we could shoot up the interrupt vectors, the BIOS RAM areas (BDA, EBDA), or shadowed option ROMs. The P for Phil also happens to also decode to push %ax. If the BIOS leaves us with a somewhat sane stack pointer, the push instruction should hopefully not mess anything up. It is part of the ZIP magic and thus unavoidable. The version field is itself actually structured, containing a decimal encoded version number, followed by an OS ID byte. If we set it to 0x000a (stored as little endian), this decodes to version 1.0 on MS DOS. 0x0a is an orb, version 1.1 would be double byte sized, version 0.8 and 0.9 would be register direct and not touch the memory. An address of BX + SI is the result of a mod-reg-r/m field with all zeros. We could try to code golf our way into consuming at least part of the flags as well, but low-valued, "harmless" opcodes that result in sane versions are sparse. Also, some version numbers change the meaning how an archiver is supposed to interpret the file. Also also, mod-reg-r/m combinations in the OS code field quickly end up as an undefined OS ID. Also also also, we have the method as well, that has to be 0x0000, which would result in a memory write if executed. We have to consume that somehow, rather than running it. So for the flags, I came up with 0x8002 (stored as little endian). The lowest, set bit has a compression method dependent meaning, currently only defined for LZMA (14), deflate (8) and implode (6). For uncompressed (method 0) there is no defined meaning (the specification just ignores that part, it doesn't use nasty words like undefined). For deflate it would mean that maximum compression was used. The MSB is specified as "reserved for use by PKWARE", whatever they chose to put there, if they ever chose anything at all. Most imporanly, the opcode 0x02 decodes to a single byte, indirect add, and in the mod-reg-r/m, the MSB tells the CPU to consume another 2 bytes of immediate DISPlacement. This is how we can get rid of the compression method. At this point, we've made it! We reached the modtime field that we can just stuff a jump into. Drawing the rest of the owl: Multiboot on foot Once we've made it past the header, we are in 16 bit real mode. We just need to go through all of the neccessary steps to set up the environment that the Multiboot code expects: Initialization (setup segments, clear scratch memory) Figure out what kind of CPU we are running on We need at least an i386, so we can actually run 32 bit code The CPUID instruction was added to the Pentium and later 486, so we can't use that We need to tickle undefined bits in the FLAGS register and watch what happens Query disk parameters, load additional boot code past the first sector We need the C/H/S geometry to sanely read past the first track For simplicity, work with LBA and convert to C/H/S bit confetti for INT 13h as needed Detect available memory Memory below 1M via INT 12h If supported, high memory via INT 15h, AX=E801h to query memory before and after the (possible) ISA memory hole at 15M If that fails, fallback to INT 15h, AH=88h to get a lump sum of available high memory If supported, get a detailed memory map via INT 15h, AX=E820h. This already uses the format specified by the Multiboot spec, just slap an extra size value in front of every entry. Turn on the A20 gate Check if memory location 0000:0600 (=0x0600) and ffff:0610 (=0x100600) overlap or not Try BIOS INT 15h, AX=2401h If that fails, try talking to the keyboard controller directly If that fails, try SYSCTL A register Load a GDT and set up 16 bit unreal mode To actually access high memory, we need to get rid of the 64k segment limits We need to stay in real-ish mode, so we can keep using INT 13h Load the rest of the archive into high memory Jump to the Multiboot entry point Re-enter protected mode, 32 bit code segment Cobble the rest of the Multiboot info struct together Leap-of-faith into highmem This might sound like a lot, but in the current version, the actual code boils down to 817 bytes. That includes all the headers (ZIP, multiboot), the rather bulky GDT. But it is still quite a lot and outside the scope of this post anyway, I might pick some interesting parts out of it for some follow-up posts (watch this space?). Through the Looking Glass The Multiboot entry code re-loads the GDT, but this time using the highmem location, and sets up a stack after the archive. The size is extracted from the Multiboot header. Knowing the start address, the C code can then iterate over itself to locate and access files in the archive. Some linker script trickery is used to tie it all into one blob, but with the GDT and Multiboot header visible from both lomem and highmem code at different locations. At this point, you might be inclined to actually read the source code in the ZIP archive. There are lots of comments trying to explain what is going on. There's a README that points out the structure of the code with suggestions where to start reading. I decided to keep it readable rather than stuff it all into a single sector. Self-modifying trickery is kept to a minimum (to safe some space, the function to enter unreal mode modifies itself, the code is run twice, courtesy of a misdirected ret, entering protected mode the first time round, leaving it again and restoring the segment registers on the second run, before returning for real). Have fun!

So, after a debugging session the other day, I was having some shower thoughts regarding early userspace and initrd.

Linux initramfs supports unpacking CPIO, a stupid, simple, standardized format. In the discussion on whether to support TAR instead, much emphasize has been put on the fact that CPIO is standardized and less fragmented.

Luckily, Linux (the kernel) includes its own tool to produce the specific variant of the standard that it happens to implement. The standard CPIO tool is possibly the most cursed archiver under the SUN.

In the old DOS/WinDOS world, ZIP was probably the most wide spread and well known archive format, being displaced to some extend by the rise of RAR during the 2000s.

Because of the design of the format, ZIP lends itself to all kinds of polyglot trickery. Way back when, self extracting ZIP archives where a thing, EXE/ZIP polyglots that can be run and unpack themselves, which is useful if you don't have an archiver installed.

I don't think I need to explain where I am going with this, here is the resulting ZIP archive I built:

Download boot.zip

It is a completely normal ZIP archive, containing its own source code needed to build itself from scratch:

$ unzip -t boot.zip
Archive:  boot.zip
    testing: boot/ZIPHEAD.COM         OK
    testing: boot/MESSAGE.TXT         OK
    testing: common/asm.h             OK
    testing: common/multiboot.h       OK
    testing: common/zip.h             OK
    testing: multiboot/console.c      OK
    testing: multiboot/console.h      OK
    testing: multiboot/multiboot.c    OK
    testing: multiboot/string.S       OK
    testing: setup/a20.S              OK
    testing: setup/disk.S             OK
    testing: setup/entry16.S          OK
    testing: setup/entry32.S          OK
    testing: setup/mbload.S           OK
    testing: setup/mem.S              OK
    testing: setup/setup.ld           OK
    testing: util/fixhdr.c            OK
    testing: util/zipglue.c           OK
    testing: util/zippack.c           OK
    testing: mk.sh                    OK
    testing: README.txt               OK
    testing: MESSAGE.txt              OK
    testing: LICENSE.txt              OK
No errors detected in compressed data of boot.zip.

A particularly interesting file here is boot/ZIPHEAD.COM, that contains executable code that is run when booting the archive.

You need to fix the execute permissions of mk.sh after unpacking, and you will need a copy of Zlib installed for the tools. Running mk.sh from it's directory should leave you with a fresh copy of the bootable ZIP archive.

The simplest way to run it, is to just pass it to Qemu direct kernel boot:

$ qemu-system-i386 -kernel boot.zip

"That's easy" you might say, "Qemu supports Multiboot, that ZIPHEAD.COM is uncompressed, at the beginning of the archive and has a Multiboot header in it!"

Yes, that's all true! But this ZIP archive also brings it's own boot loader along. You can try putting it on a floppy and throw that in front of Qemu:

$ dd if=/dev/zero of=floppy.img count=2880
$ dd if=boot.zip of=floppy.img conv=notrunc
$ qemu-system-i386 -fda floppy.img

The first 512 bytes of the archive contain a valid boot sector that loads some more code from the second sector and then bootstraps itself into highmem with the A20 enabled and 32 bit protected mode set up.

You can also put it on a hard drive too, it detects what INT 13h drive it's been loaded from and dutifully queries the disk geometry.

If you care to try, you can also dump it on a real floppy and stuff it into a PC:

That's a Pentium MMX by the way, but I also tried an i486 DX2 and an Am386DX-40, just to be sure. My 486 had me hold my breath for a moment, it has a spectacularly slow floppy drive. The text on screen is from the file boot/MESSAGE.TXT

"But that's not special either" you might respond, "ZIPs are read from the back, you can just put anything you want in front, so you put a boot sector there!"

That is sadly not quite true anymore, I'll get to that. But for now, lets take a look at the first couple bytes of that archive together and we'll see the real party trick:

$ xxd -g 1 -l 128 boot.zip
00000000: 50 4b 03 04 0a 00 02 80 00 00 eb 44 e4 2e 41 0f  PK.........D..A.
00000010: 01 8f 0a 09 00 00 0a 09 00 00 10 00 00 00 62 6f  ..............bo
00000020: 6f 74 2f 5a 49 50 48 45 41 44 2e 43 4f 4d 00 90  ot/ZIPHEAD.COM..
00000030: 02 b0 ad 1b 03 00 01 00 fb 4f 51 e4 30 00 10 00  .........OQ.0...
00000040: 00 00 10 00 bd 72 10 00 bd 72 10 00 31 03 10 00  .....r...r..1...
00000050: fa fc 31 c0 89 c4 8e d8 8e c0 8e d0 ea 61 7c 00  ..1..........a|.
00000060: 00 bf 00 06 b9 00 02 f3 aa 88 16 98 06 be 0f 7d  ...............}
00000070: e8 8c 00 b8 00 f0 89 c1 50 9d 9c 58 a8 02 74 4a  ........P..X..tJ

The ASCII P stands for Phil ( not Picard ), as in Phil Katz, followed by 03h and 04h. What you are looking at, is a completely valid ZIP local file header for boot/ZIPHEAD.COM

Oh, and those other bytes there after the ZIP header: 02 b0 ad 1b, if you flip them around to human endian, it reads 1BADB002. That's the Multiboot magic :-)

The 16 bit real mode code starts right after the Multiboot header, at offset 00000050. If you are feeling a little confused, so is the file utility:

2,19,7), end-CHS (0x388,254,6), startsector 2147916342, 243810273 sectors; parti

If you take a closer look at the first line of the hex dump, you might be able to spot the jump instruction that makes this little magic trick possible. Luckily, Phil Katz' initials are valid opcodes. The Multiboot entry point is much further into the file at offset 00000331.

ZIP Archives Revisited

Here's a picture you probably recognize from the Wikipedia article about the ZIP format . This here is a local copy, Wikimedia Commons hosts the original with attribution and licensing information .

Much like a TAR or CPIO archive, a ZIP file is an amalgamation of tightly packed files with a short header in front, specifying the full file path and other meta data:

typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t version;
	uint16_t flags;
	uint16_t method;
	uint16_t modtime;
	uint16_t moddate;
	uint32_t checksum;
	uint32_t compsize;
	uint32_t origsize;
	uint16_t namelength;
	uint16_t extralength;
	char name[namelength];
	uint8_t extra[extralength];
} __attribute__((packed)) zip_entry_t;

The timestamps are DOS datetime, the checksum is a CRC-32, there are no attributes or permission bits, we are thoroughly in DOS land. Directories are implied by the file paths.

Nit pick Yes, I know, the central directory has a field where "internal" and "external" attributes can be stored, whose meaning depends on the OS ID byte in the version field. Later versions of the format added an extension to support directories. Good luck making use of that in a portable way that can be understood by different archivers across different WinDOS versions and Unix clones.

Unlike TAR or CPIO, there is a central directory in the end, with a listing of all of the file headers and back references to the file in the archive. Unlike traditional file formats that have are started by a header, ZIP is terminated by a footer.

The reason for this is twofold:

  • the archive can be generated in a single, forward pass (collecting the directory in memory).
  • Accessing a single file in the archive can be done quickly, by looking through the directory and going directly to the file.

That last part was especially important in the days when ZIP archives would be split over several floppies. To access a file, just scan the directory on the last floppy, then tell the user what floppy to insert to get the file.

By comparison, accessing a file in a tarball requires linearly scanning over the whole thing (which, on the other hand, is preferable for tape drives , where TAR originates).

Polyglot Trickery

ZIP archives are meant to be read from the back, the footer points to the central directory, the directory points to the files. In theory, the archiver shouldn't care if there happens to be a gap between two files, containing something else or if there is something else in the front of the archive, like a file header for a different file format.

The local file headers also supports up to 64k of "extra" stuff between the header and the file data, the footer has "comment" at the end, also up to 64k.

If you look at the footer for a second, you might spot an interesting design flaw:

typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t disknum;
	uint16_t diskstart;
	uint16_t num_dir_entries;
	uint16_t total_dir_entries;
	uint32_t dir_size;
	uint32_t dir_start;
	uint16_t comment_length;
	uint8_t comment[comment_length];
} __attribute__((packed)) zip_end_t;

it is variable size, an archiver needs to find it looking from the back, but the magic and the size are both stored before the variable sized comment field. Ask yourself this for a moment: how would you implement this in an archiver? Demanding that there is no comment? Reading the last 64k plus some change and scanning it? From which direction? What if there is another valid footer inside the comment field of the footer? Depending on how an implementation deals with this, a specifically crafted archive can appear to contain different files when viewed with different archivers.

Trying to make the format extensible ended up building a whole lot of foot guns in there. And we are not even talking about the plethora of extensions that have been tacked on to the official specification over the years.

Many modern implementations decided to save themselves a lot of headaches and just treat ZIP archives the same way as tarballs, linearly scanning them from the front instead. They expect the archive to start with a local header, skipping by the size MUST lead to the next entry or finally, the central directory. They reject any archives where this is not possible. This effectively prevents a lot of polyglot trick fuckery, but at the cost of rendering possibly valid archives unreadable.

For the self booting ZIP archive, the challenge thus becomes: the archive MUST start with a local file header, there cannot be any gaps, everything must be properly contained inside files.

The easy part: Multiboot

Anybody who has ever looked at a DIY toy OS tutorial has probably stumbled across The Multiboot Specification , the possibly easiest and most beginner friendly way to get a program running on bare metal x86.

The multiboot spec originates in the GNU/FSF ecosystem and is implemented by boot loaders like GRUB or Qemu direct kernel boot. SYSLINUX supports it via a plugin. There is a draft for an over engineered 2nd version, that also supports MIPS, but this is of no concert to us here.

A Multiboot 1 compliant kernel simply contains the magic value 0x1BADB002 somewhere in the first in the first 8k. This is followed by flags and a checksum (all 3 must add up to zero). Depending on the flags, additional fields may follow.

The kernel itself can be an ELF file from which the loader extracts load address and entry point. The kernel is run in 32 bit protected mode with flat segments (base=0, limit=4G) and the A20 gate enabled.

Nit pick The specification actually doesn't mandate ELF, but rather "an ordinary 32-bit executable file in whatever file format the operating system normally uses.", it then goes on to specify optional fields in the info struct for either ELF or a.out. In theory, it should also be possible for a boot loader to only support PE and not be in violation of the spec.

Alternatively to a plain old ELF file, the kernel can also specify the memory layout manually (indicated via a flag), allowing flat binaries or other file formats to be loaded. The extended header looks like this:

typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint32_t flags;
	uint32_t checksum;
	uint32_t hdr_addr;
	uint32_t load_addr;
	uint32_t load_end_addr;
	uint32_t bss_end_addr;
	uint32_t entry_point;
} mb_header_t;

The hdr_addr specifies the in-memory address of the header after loading the file, using this and the file offset where the header was found, the other addresses can be converted back to file offsets by the loader.

This way, the load_addr and load_end_addr are used to figure out what parts of the file to load where into memory. If the bss_end_addr is past that, the loader zero-fills it, before finally jumping to entry_point to run the kernel.

The Multiboot compliant loader also sets up a structure with system information (e.g. memory map, APM tables), kernel command line, etc… and passes the pointer to the kernel (via register EBX, magic value 0x2BADB002 in EAX).

Making a Multiboot bootable ZIP archive is trivial. Simply pack a flat binary with a Multiboot header as uncompressed file binary, make sure it is at the beginning and the addresses line up. An external tool can then fix up the headers, so that the whole archive is loaded.

For any practical applications, it would make sense to stop right here, but we're not here for "practical" or "sane".

Making it BIOS bootable

On an IBM compatible machine, the BIOS iterates over the installed drives, loads the first sector from each (to location 0x7c00), until it finds one where the first sector ends with 0xaa55. It then jumps to the first byte.

Disks that are formatted with a filesystem, typically have a header in the beginning that starts with a jump instruction across the header into the bootstrap code that follows. The DOS MBR format opts to instead store the partition table at the end of the first sector and all the code in the front.

If we stuff a BIOS boot signature into the ZIP archive, at least parts of the ZIP local file header will be executed, the first few bytes are a mandated magic value and we cannot just put a jump instruction there.

The puzzle exercise now becomes, filling the header fields with values that make sense but also happen to be valid 8086 opcodes. At least, until we hit something that can be abused as a free-form field that we can stuff a jump into.

Let's take a look at that hex dump again:

00000000: 50 4b 03 04 0a 00 02 80 00 00 eb 44 e4 2e 41 0f  PK.........D..A.
00000010: 01 8f 0a 09 00 00 0a 09 00 00 10 00 00 00 62 6f  ..............bo
00000020: 6f 74 2f 5a 49 50 48 45 41 44 2e 43 4f 4d 00 90  ot/ZIPHEAD.COM..

I've tried to highlight the relevant header up to the jump instruction: 0xeb is a relative jump with a single byte immediate argument.

If we take a look again at the header structure, we can make out what fields those bytes correspond to:

typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t version;
	uint16_t flags;
	uint16_t method;
	uint16_t modtime;
	………

The timestamp is the first best place where we can put a jump instruction. The 0xeb relative jump works out to 8:30-ish in the morning, give or take the jump distance.

The two bytes in front of the modtime are compression method. We really, really want to have 0x0000 here, i.e. uncompressed, so that an archiver doesn't choke on the file data.

The first four bytes are the magic value of the format, we don't have any choice what to put here either, it has to be "PK\03\04". The version and flags fields are the only places where we have some creative freedom.

If we run the file through a dissassembler and take a look at the first few bytes, we'll end up with this:

$ objdump -D -m i8086 -b binary ./boot.zip

./boot.zip:     file format binary


Disassembly of section .data:

00000000 <.data>:
       0:       50                      push   %ax
       1:       4b                      dec    %bx
       2:       03 04                   add    (%si),%ax
       4:       0a 00                   or     (%bx,%si),%al
       6:       02 80 00 00             add    0x0(%bx,%si),%al
       a:       eb 44                   jmp    0x50

This is AT&T syntax, source operands are left, destination on the right. We use GNU tools in this household, deal with it.

Anything that just fiddles around with a register doesn't really hurt us. Same goes for memory reads. We don't have memory protection, no matter what we access, there won't be any faults, the only memory mapped hardware around should be the frame buffer.

Memory writes are another story. Worst case, we could shoot up the interrupt vectors, the BIOS RAM areas (BDA, EBDA), or shadowed option ROMs.

The P for Phil also happens to also decode to push %ax. If the BIOS leaves us with a somewhat sane stack pointer, the push instruction should hopefully not mess anything up. It is part of the ZIP magic and thus unavoidable.

The version field is itself actually structured, containing a decimal encoded version number, followed by an OS ID byte. If we set it to 0x000a (stored as little endian), this decodes to version 1.0 on MS DOS.

0x0a is an orb, version 1.1 would be double byte sized, version 0.8 and 0.9 would be register direct and not touch the memory. An address of BX + SI is the result of a mod-reg-r/m field with all zeros.

We could try to code golf our way into consuming at least part of the flags as well, but low-valued, "harmless" opcodes that result in sane versions are sparse. Also, some version numbers change the meaning how an archiver is supposed to interpret the file. Also also, mod-reg-r/m combinations in the OS code field quickly end up as an undefined OS ID. Also also also, we have the method as well, that has to be 0x0000, which would result in a memory write if executed. We have to consume that somehow, rather than running it.

So for the flags, I came up with 0x8002 (stored as little endian). The lowest, set bit has a compression method dependent meaning, currently only defined for LZMA (14), deflate (8) and implode (6). For uncompressed (method 0) there is no defined meaning (the specification just ignores that part, it doesn't use nasty words like undefined). For deflate it would mean that maximum compression was used.

The MSB is specified as "reserved for use by PKWARE", whatever they chose to put there, if they ever chose anything at all. Most imporanly, the opcode 0x02 decodes to a single byte, indirect add, and in the mod-reg-r/m, the MSB tells the CPU to consume another 2 bytes of immediate DISPlacement. This is how we can get rid of the compression method.

At this point, we've made it! We reached the modtime field that we can just stuff a jump into.

Drawing the rest of the owl: Multiboot on foot

Once we've made it past the header, we are in 16 bit real mode. We just need to go through all of the neccessary steps to set up the environment that the Multiboot code expects:

  • Initialization (setup segments, clear scratch memory)
  • Figure out what kind of CPU we are running on
    • We need at least an i386, so we can actually run 32 bit code
    • The CPUID instruction was added to the Pentium and later 486, so we can't use that
    • We need to tickle undefined bits in the FLAGS register and watch what happens
  • Query disk parameters, load additional boot code past the first sector We need the C/H/S geometry to sanely read past the first track For simplicity, work with LBA and convert to C/H/S bit confetti for INT 13h as needed
  • Detect available memory Memory below 1M via INT 12h If supported, high memory via INT 15h, AX=E801h to query memory before and after the (possible) ISA memory hole at 15M If that fails, fallback to INT 15h, AH=88h to get a lump sum of available high memory If supported, get a detailed memory map via INT 15h, AX=E820h. This already uses the format specified by the Multiboot spec, just slap an extra size value in front of every entry.
  • Turn on the A20 gate Check if memory location 0000:0600 (=0x0600) and ffff:0610 (=0x100600) overlap or not Try BIOS INT 15h, AX=2401h If that fails, try talking to the keyboard controller directly If that fails, try SYSCTL A register
  • Load a GDT and set up 16 bit unreal mode To actually access high memory, we need to get rid of the 64k segment limits We need to stay in real-ish mode, so we can keep using INT 13h
  • Load the rest of the archive into high memory
  • Jump to the Multiboot entry point Re-enter protected mode, 32 bit code segment Cobble the rest of the Multiboot info struct together Leap-of-faith into highmem

This might sound like a lot, but in the current version, the actual code boils down to 817 bytes. That includes all the headers (ZIP, multiboot), the rather bulky GDT. But it is still quite a lot and outside the scope of this post anyway, I might pick some interesting parts out of it for some follow-up posts (watch this space?).

Through the Looking Glass

The Multiboot entry code re-loads the GDT, but this time using the highmem location, and sets up a stack after the archive. The size is extracted from the Multiboot header. Knowing the start address, the C code can then iterate over itself to locate and access files in the archive.

Some linker script trickery is used to tie it all into one blob, but with the GDT and Multiboot header visible from both lomem and highmem code at different locations.

At this point, you might be inclined to actually read the source code in the ZIP archive. There are lots of comments trying to explain what is going on.

There's a README that points out the structure of the code with suggestions where to start reading. I decided to keep it readable rather than stuff it all into a single sector. Self-modifying trickery is kept to a minimum (to safe some space, the function to enter unreal mode modifies itself, the code is run twice, courtesy of a misdirected ret, entering protected mode the first time round, leaving it again and restoring the segment registers on the second run, before returning for real).
